prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "QUALCOMM INC/DE" (ticker QCOM). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)

   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))

   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)

   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Qualcomm is a top dog in premium Android chips and cellular patents, but its core smartphone market is mature, the stock has lagged (about 4.8% a year total return since early 2021), and the market already calls it fairly valued rather than overvalued. It fits Rule Breaker traits only partly, with its AI data center push as the main emerging-industry angle.
summaries.buffett: The patent-licensing toll on almost every 4G/5G phone, high returns on capital (ROIC about 26%) and strong free cash flow ($12.8B in FY2025) are Buffett-like, and it pays a growing dividend. Against that, results are cyclical (revenue fell 19% in FY2023), technology change is fast and big customers like Apple are building their own chips, which makes long-run earnings hard to predict.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the hard-to-copy modem know-how and patent moat but would worry, thinking backwards, about customer concentration, Apple and Samsung in-sourcing, China exposure and the need to win new markets against NVIDIA and Broadcom. At roughly 16-17 times forward earnings it is a fair price for a good, not great, business.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would class Qualcomm as a cyclical stalwart: the story is that automotive (up 61% year over year in Q3 FY2026), IoT and data centers replace shrinking Apple and Android handset revenue. With EPS expected to fall about 13% in FY2026, the P/E is well above the growth rate, so it fails his PEG test for now.
summaries.fisher: Qualcomm scores well on Fisher's R&D points, spending about $9B a year (20% of sales) with results such as Snapdragon, 5G modems and the Digital Chassis, and management keeps launching products as phones mature. Weaker points are falling gross margins (60.7% in FY2020 to 55.4% in FY2025) and growth that has stalled since FY2022.
summaries.graham: Qualcomm is large and has paid dividends every year since 2003, and EPS rose from $3.22 (FY2015) to $5.01 (FY2025), but it posted a net loss in FY2018 and trades at about 20 times trailing earnings and 6.6 times book. It does not meet Graham's defensive-investor price tests.
summaries.thiel: Qualcomm once had near-monopoly technology in CDMA and still controls essential cellular patents, but today its chips compete with MediaTek, Apple and Samsung and are not ten times better. Its new markets (PCs, cars, data centers) are crowded, so it fits Thiel's monopoly ideal only partly.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price with an AI tailwind; Qualcomm is cheap at about 16 times forward earnings with a 5.7% free-cash-flow yield, and it has two hyperscaler custom-silicon wins. But consensus expects revenue to fall about 3% in FY2026 and grow under 5% in FY2027, so it lacks the growth he prefers.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller wants accelerating earnings and rising estimates; Qualcomm's FY2026 EPS is expected to fall about 13% amid a memory-driven handset slump and Apple modem losses. Possible catalysts are data center revenue from the December 2026 quarter and the Arm royalty ruling, but the trend is not clearly upward yet.
summaries.smith: Qualcomm has Terry Smith-style qualities in high gross margins (55%), high returns on capital and strong cash conversion, but sales have not compounded (FY2025 revenue barely above FY2022) and earnings are cyclical. It is a good business at a fair price rather than a consistent compounder.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Qualcomm screens reasonably: ROIC around 26% and an earnings yield of about 5.5% (EV/EBIT about 18). That is decent but not top-decile for a formula that favours cheap, high-return businesses.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs are a good business, talented owner-minded managers and reinvestment opportunities. Qualcomm's licensing and chip franchise is good and Amon is a capable engineer-CEO, but most free cash flow goes to buybacks and dividends rather than high-return reinvestment, and insiders own only about 0.05%.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks low-risk, high-uncertainty bets on temporarily depressed businesses; Qualcomm's handset slump and memory crunch may be temporary, and its $14B of operating cash flow limits permanent-loss risk. But at about 16 times forward earnings it is not priced at the deep discount Dhandho investing requires.
summaries.wood: Qualcomm takes part in ARK-style themes such as on-device AI, autonomous driving and robotics, but it is a mature incumbent whose core handset market is shrinking, not a pure disruptive-innovation platform. ARK would likely see it as a supplier to innovation rather than a leading disruptor.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and pricing power; Qualcomm generates plenty of cash and has a licensing moat, but handset cyclicality and customer concentration make it less predictable. The heavy debt load ($15.3B) against $8.3B of cash is manageable given cash flow.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for scale-economies-shared businesses that grow stronger over time; Qualcomm instead raises prices (double-digit increases announced in 2026) and its market position has eroded as Apple and Samsung in-source chips. It does not fit the Nomad model well.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed companies attacking huge markets with technology that solves big problems; Qualcomm did exactly that with CDMA and mobile internet, and its new data center and automotive markets are large. Today it is a mature incumbent rather than an early-stage market creator.
summaries.nash: Qualcomm passes Nash's quality screens on margins (operating margin about 24-28%), cash flow and profitability, but fails key kill criteria: debt ($15.3B) exceeds cash ($8.3B) and revenue growth is below 10% and expected negative in FY2026. Its Nash scorecard total is about 55 and his DCF gives about $129 per share versus a $172 price.

momentum.evidence: The stock closed at $172.11 on Oct 16, 2026, up only about 5.6% over 52 weeks and roughly flat year to date after peaking near $258 in May 2026, lagging the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Cristiano Amon is a respected 30-year Qualcomm engineer-executive and the company partners with Samsung, Meta, BMW and hyperscalers, but it has no famous anchor investor beyond index funds and institutions (about 84% institutional ownership).

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly rate it Hold (23 of 37) with a median target of $175 near the price, and it trades at about 16-17 times forward earnings; it is seen as fairly valued, not overvalued.

simple.evidence: The business is understandable: it sells chips (QCT, $38.4B in FY2025) and licenses cellular patents (QTL, $5.6B), mostly to phone makers.

b2.evidence: It has been consistently profitable except FY2018 (a $4.86B net loss from tax reform and the NXP deal termination), but revenue swings with the handset cycle, falling 19% in FY2023.

integrity.evidence: Disclosure is clear and capital returns are sizeable ($12.6B in FY2025), but the company has faced past antitrust fines over licensing practices and insiders own only about 0.05% of shares.

b6.evidence: Acquisitions have been mostly targeted tuck-ins (Nuvia 2021, Alphawave about $2.4B in Dec 2025, Arduino, Modular), though its data center push follows a crowded AI trend.

roic.evidence: Trailing ROIC is about 26% and ROE about 34% (StockAnalysis), with interest coverage of about 15x, so returns do not depend on leverage.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 operating cash flow was $14.01B and capex $1.19B, giving about $12.8B of free cash flow, a 29% FCF margin and well above GAAP net income of $5.54B (depressed by a non-cash tax charge).

b10.evidence: Ten-year total return of about 13.2% a year trailed the S&P 500 and revenue has been flat since FY2022, so retained earnings have not created proportional market value.

safety.evidence: A Nash-style DCF using its own 3-year average growth (1.2%) and FCF margin (28.4%) at a 12% discount rate gives about $129 per share, below the $172 price.

fairprice.evidence: About 16.4 times FY2026 consensus non-GAAP EPS of $10.48 and a 5.7% FCF yield is reasonable for its quality, but EPS is expected to fall in FY2026 and FY2027.

mu5.evidence: Failure risks include Apple and Samsung in-sourcing, Chinese OEMs designing their own chips, US-China export controls and Arm licensing disputes, although the patent portfolio and diversified chip lines limit the chance of collapse.

reinvest.evidence: It is reinvesting in automotive, PCs and data centers (targeting $40B non-handset revenue by FY2029), but most free cash flow is returned through buybacks and dividends rather than high-return reinvestment.

ly2.evidence: It fits Lynch's cyclical/stalwart category with a simple story: grow cars, IoT and data centers fast enough to offset a shrinking handset and Apple business.

ly3.evidence: With a trailing P/E around 20 and consensus EPS expected to fall about 13% in FY2026, the P/E is far above the earnings growth rate.

runway.evidence: Automotive grew from $975M (FY2021) to $3.96B (FY2025) and data center revenue starts in late 2026, but handset revenue (63% of FY2025 sales) is expected to decline.

ly7.evidence: Buybacks cut diluted shares from 1,149M in FY2020 to 1,069M in the June 2026 quarter, but insider ownership is only about 0.05% and insiders are not notable buyers.

ly8.evidence: Qualcomm is a widely followed mega-cap covered by 37 analysts.

fi2.evidence: As smartphones mature, management has launched Snapdragon X PC chips, the Snapdragon Digital Chassis for cars and AI200/AI250 data center accelerators (announced Oct 2025).

fi3.evidence: Roughly $9B of yearly R&D has produced industry-leading 5G modems, Snapdragon 8 Elite processors and an automotive business with double-digit growth for 23 consecutive quarters.

fi4.evidence: It wins design slots at nearly every major Android OEM and many carmakers, and its licensing team signs nearly every handset maker, but Apple and Huawei business has been lost.

longterm.evidence: It keeps R&D around 20% of revenue and pursues multi-year bets like data centers and 6G even as FY2026 earnings decline.

gr1.evidence: Market cap is about $184B with FY2025 revenue of $44.3B.

ni10.evidence: Qualcomm reported a net loss of $4.86B in FY2018, within the last ten fiscal years.

gr4.evidence: Qualcomm has paid a dividend every year since 2003 (23 years), currently $3.68 a share annualized.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $3.22 in FY2015 to $5.01 in FY2025 (+56%), and non-GAAP EPS was $12.03 in FY2025.

gr6.evidence: At $172 the stock is about 20 times trailing GAAP earnings, above Graham's 15x limit.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 20 times P/B of about 6.6 gives roughly 130, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Snapdragon and its modems lead in performance but are not ten times better than MediaTek Dimensity or Apple's chips.

timing.evidence: On-device AI, software-defined cars and AI inference in data centers are well timed, but 2026 handset demand is weak because of memory shortages.

th3.evidence: It started by dominating CDMA and grew into the leading premium smartphone chip and patent company, but its newer markets are being entered from scratch against strong incumbents.

team.evidence: Cristiano Amon and the team are experienced and credible, but not a founder-led or exceptional team by Thiel's standard.

th5.evidence: Deep relationships with every major Android OEM, carmakers and carriers, plus a licensing team with agreements across the industry, give it strong distribution.

durable.evidence: Its patent and modem know-how should remain relevant through 5G Advanced and 6G, but customer in-sourcing has already cut its smartphone SoC share from 30% (Q2 2024) to 23% (Q2 2026).

th7.evidence: Its growth areas (AI PCs, cars, data centers) are targeted by many competitors, so the opportunity is not one others overlook.

trend.evidence: It benefits from on-device AI and has two hyperscaler custom-silicon wins, but it is not yet a leading AI beneficiary like NVIDIA or Broadcom.

dr1.evidence: Consensus FY2026 non-GAAP EPS of $10.48 is down about 13% from $12.03 and FY2027 is expected lower at $10.19.

dr2.evidence: Data center revenue starting in the December 2026 quarter, price increases and a recovering Chinese handset business could make it look better by 2028, but Apple revenue is falling about 50% sequentially into that quarter.

dr4.evidence: Lower rates help valuations, but memory price inflation and weak consumer electronics demand are hurting its handset business.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include data center revenue ramping through FY2027, the Delaware judge's Arm royalty ruling, the Huawei license closing and FY2026 results in November 2026.

dr7.evidence: Falling earnings estimates, a mostly Hold consensus and handset headwinds make it hard to justify as a high-conviction concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 55.4% in FY2025, high for a chip company, though down from 60.7% in FY2020.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $10.4B on a $184B market cap gives a 5.7% FCF yield, attractive for its quality.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 18 (EV $191B), an earnings yield of about 5.5%, moderate rather than high.

pa2.evidence: The memory-cost-driven handset slump looks temporary, but losing Apple modem business is permanent.

pa4.evidence: With $14B of annual operating cash flow, an Altman Z-score around 5.9 and a large patent portfolio, the risk of permanent loss of capital is small.

wo1.evidence: It is a leader in on-device AI processing for phones and PCs and is entering AI inference in data centers, but it is not the AI leader.

wo2.evidence: It is raising prices by double digits in 2026 to offset higher input costs rather than cutting costs to unlock new demand.

wo3.evidence: It touches AI, autonomous driving, robotics and connectivity, but these are add-ons to a handset-centred business.

wo4.evidence: Management's FY2029 target of $40B non-handset revenue would be meaningful growth but not a many-fold increase in its addressable market.

ac3.evidence: It is not exposed to commodity prices directly, but memory prices, foundry costs, China trade policy and consumer demand affect it significantly.

ns1.evidence: Qualcomm raises prices and royalties rather than sharing scale savings with customers.

ns4.evidence: Automotive and data center growth could strengthen it, but its smartphone share is eroding as major customers in-source chips.

va2.evidence: Its modems and processors solve the hard problem of fast, power-efficient wireless connectivity and computing for billions of devices.

tn1.evidence: It sells into AI and connected cars, but as a smartphone-era incumbent retrofitting into data centers rather than a company built for the AI infrastructure layer.

tn2.evidence: The market still values it as a phone-chip company at about 16 times forward earnings, while management targets $40B non-handset revenue by FY2029, a possible story gap if data centers ramp.

tn3.evidence: It is a $184B US company, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable and revenue grew in FY2024 and FY2025, but debt ($15.27B) exceeds cash ($8.30B) and FY2026 revenue is expected to dip, so it passes about two of three.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive each quarter, but debt exceeded cash and marketable securities at each recent quarter-end ($15.27B vs $8.30B at June 28, 2026).

tn6.evidence: Trailing revenue is about $44.07B, flat to FY2025's $44.28B, and FY2026 consensus is down about 3%.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 0% plus a trailing FCF margin of about 24% totals roughly 24, below 40.

tn8.evidence: Trailing revenue slipped slightly while R&D and SG&A rose (Q3 FY2026 R&D $2.61B vs $2.23B a year earlier).

tn9.evidence: It fails two instant kills: more debt ($15.27B) than cash ($8.30B), and revenue growth below 10% and falling.

tn10.evidence: It faces the Arm licensing litigation (Oct 2026 verdict, royalty issues pending before the judge), US-China export-control risk and continuing antitrust scrutiny of licensing.

tn11.evidence: Qualcomm provides wireless processors and essential patents that help device makers build connected, AI-capable phones, PCs and cars, and charges per-chip prices plus royalties on device sales.

tn13.evidence: Score about 55/130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin (about 24%) 5, short interest (3.3%) 10, institutional ownership (84%) 10, revenue vs expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 0, and 5 each for moat, CEO, pricing power, secular trend, culture and talent.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in FY2023, gross margin declined from 60.7% to 55.4% over five years, and debt exceeded cash in recent years, although free cash flow stayed positive.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 15x, the current ratio 2.0 and liabilities about 1.1x equity, but assets excluding $14.27B goodwill ($43.1B) are only about 1.45x total liabilities ($29.7B).

tn18.evidence: Amon has executed on diversification (automotive revenue up about fourfold since FY2021) but has been CEO only since 2021, is not a founder and has not made notable open-market purchases.

tn20.evidence: It beat non-GAAP EPS estimates in five of the last six quarters, with Q3 FY2026 ($2.21) about $0.01 below consensus, per OpenCapital.

tn21.evidence: No fraud or auditor issues, but gross margin has declined over five years and it has made several acquisitions in 2025-2026 (Alphawave, Arduino, Modular).

tn22.evidence: It has $44B of revenue, strong cash flow and a shrinking share count, so it avoids the hype trap.

tn24.evidence: A 5.7% FCF yield at a ~10-12% required return implies roughly 4-6% long-run growth, above the near-zero revenue growth it has delivered since FY2022.

tn25.evidence: Nash's DCF (1.2% growth, 28.4% FCF margin, 12% discount, 4% terminal, plus cash minus debt) gives about $129 per share, below $172.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E is about 16-17 on falling EPS (FY2027 consensus $10.19 vs $10.48), so the PEG is not meaningful or above 1 even though the P/E is below many chip peers.
